title: [Bounty $750] Fix remaining sharded scale_mask_softmax mask handling issues
author: jberkowitzTT
body:
📝 Background

ttnn.scale_mask_softmax_in_place with SoftmaxShardedMultiCoreProgramConfig can hang or read incorrect mask values when the input shard layout and mask shape/specification do not align. These cases can break correctness in sharded attention workloads and may hang the device instead of returning a clear validation error.

An open change already addresses the causal-mask case where a shard is shorter than or not divisible by the mask height, and the causal mask/input batch-size mismatch. This bounty is for the remaining issues below; coordinate with that change and do not duplicate its scope: [PR #63692](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/pull/63692).

🎯 What Success Looks Like

A row-major mask combined with is_causal_mask=True is either handled correctly or rejected during validation with a clear error before device execution; it must not hang.

Causal interleaved mask readers wrap rows using the mask’s height, not the input width. Non-square causal masks produce correct results without out-of-bounds reads.

Mask addressing remains correct when a shard crosses a batch boundary; the batch cursor must not advance early or read beyond the mask tensor.

A sharded mask with an incompatible shard specification (including shard orientation) is rejected clearly or handled correctly; it must not silently read a different core’s shard.

Add regression tests for each addressed case, covering valid configurations and invalid configurations as appropriate. Compare supported outputs against a PyTorch reference.

Existing relevant sharded and causal softmax tests continue to pass, and existing supported configurations retain their behavior.

💡 Problem to Solve

The sharded softmax factory, mask readers, and validation do not consistently enforce or honor the assumptions used to walk masks:

A row-major mask with is_causal_mask=True can select a reader that does not follow the causal compute’s per-row mask consumption, causing a hang.

Causal interleaved readers can wrap mask rows using the input width rather than the mask height, leading to incorrect/out-of-bounds reads for non-square masks.

When a shard spans a batch boundary, integer division in the per-batch core calculation can make mask addressing advance to the next batch too early.

Validation checks mask layout and padded shape but does not ensure that a sharded mask’s shard specification matches the input’s expected distribution.

author: brianp
body:
## Bounty: L2 opens the "set a PIN" flow while the L1 wallet is still loading

**Tier:** S — 15,000 XTM

### Description

If you click the L2 sidebar button before the L1 wallet has finished loading, Universe asks you to set a PIN even when one is already set. If you enter a PIN anyway, it fails with "A PIN is already set for this wallet".

The cause is in the frontend. `openL2()` in `src/store/actions/l2OpenActions.ts` reads `useWalletStore.is_pin_locked` and opens the `l2_pin_required` (create PIN) dialog when it's `false`. That flag defaults to `false` and is only set when the wallet setup phase emits it (`src-tauri/src/setup/phase_wallet.rs:239`, `emit_pin_locked`). Until then, the app can't tell "no PIN" apart from "not loaded yet".

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] With a PIN already set, clicking the L2 button while the L1 wallet is still loading never opens the create-PIN dialog
- [ ] While the PIN state is unknown, the L2 button either waits or is disabled with a loading indication, and once the wallet has loaded it goes to the normal unlock/PIN-entry flow
- [ ] A wallet that really has no PIN still gets the create-PIN dialog, both before and after loading finishes
- [ ] Any other UI that uses `is_pin_locked` to tell whether a PIN is set (e.g. `L2Wallet.tsx` burn button, `L2WalletCard.tsx`, `SendModal.tsx`, `VerifySeedPhrase.tsx`) doesn't treat "not loaded yet" as "no PIN"
- [ ] Unit tests cover the loading state (extend `l2OpenActions.test.ts` and/or `L2WalletCard.test.tsx`)
- [ ] The PR includes a short screen recording of the fixed behaviour: launch with a PIN set and click L2 during wallet load

### Context

- Entry point: `src/containers/navigation/Sidebars/buttons/L2Button.tsx` → `openL2()` in `src/store/actions/l2OpenActions.ts`
- PIN state source: `src-tauri/src/setup/phase_wallet.rs` (`PinManager::pin_locked()` → `EventsEmitter::emit_pin_locked`)
- Backend error text: `src-tauri/src/internal_wallet.rs:667`

## Bounty: Scheduled mining window doesn't apply its mode when mining is already running

**Tier:** S — 15,000 XTM

### Description

When a scheduled mining window starts while you're already mining, the UI switches to the scheduled mode (e.g. Ludicrous), but the miners keep running with the old settings (e.g. Eco). If mining was stopped when the window starts, it mines in the scheduled mode correctly.

The `Mine` branch in `src-tauri/src/event_scheduler.rs` (around line 1096) saves the mode with `set_selected_mining_mode` and then calls `CpuManager::start_mining()` / `GpuManager::start_mining()`. Both return early when the miner is already running (`src-tauri/src/mining/cpu/manager.rs:174`, `src-tauri/src/mining/gpu/manager.rs:354`), so the new mode never reaches the miners. - [ ] The PR includes log excerpts from a manual test: mine in Eco, schedule a Ludicrous window, and show the miners restarting with the new thread count when the window starts

## Bounty: MCP server gives no error when the configured port is already in use

**Tier:** S — 15,000 XTM

### Description

If you set the MCP server port (Settings → MCP Server → Advanced) to a port another process is already using, the server correctly refuses to start, but the panel just shows **Stopped**. The panel says nothing about the port, and the log only has `MCP server stopped` / `MCP server shut down cleanly`. To the user it looks like the server died for no reason.

## Bounty: Linux Flatpak copy to clipboard fails silently under Wayland

**Tier:** S — 15,000 XTM

### Description

In the Linux Flatpak under a Wayland session, every copy button does nothing. Copy Address never switches to its copied state and nothing reaches the clipboard. The clipboard plugin returns:

```
Unknown error while interacting with the clipboard: X11 server connection timed out because it was unreachable
```

The Flatpak manifest (`flatpak/com.tari.universe.yml`) uses `--socket=wayland` plus `--socket=fallback-x11`, so on Wayland the sandbox gets no `DISPLAY`. `arboard`'s Wayland path (`wl-clipboard-rs`) needs the privileged data-control protocol, which the compositor seems to withhold from sandboxed clients, so it falls back to X11 and fails. `useCopyToClipboard` only sets `isCopied` when `writeText` succeeds, so the failure is invisible. That's especially bad for seed words, where users assume the copy worked.

Seen on Pop!_OS COSMIC (Wayland) with runtime `org.gnome.Platform//50`. Not yet checked on GNOME or KDE.

- [ ] The sandbox is **not** widened with `--socket=x11` or similar. Writing from the webview (`navigator.clipboard.writeText`, which uses WebKitGTK's GTK clipboard) or another approach that doesn't widen the sandbox is preferred
- [ ] If a copy fails, the user sees an error (e.g. a toast) instead of nothing happening

### Description

CPU mining tops out at 64 threads on Windows machines that have more than 64 logical cores. A user with 128 threads reported that only 64 were ever used, no matter what thread count they selected. The goal of this bounty is simple to state and hard to prove: **make Tari Universe actually use more than 64 threads on a Windows machine that has more than 64 logical cores.**

Windows splits machines with more than 64 logical processors into "processor groups" of at most 64 each, and a process that isn't group-aware only gets scheduled onto one group. On top of that, Rust's `std::thread::available_parallelism()` (which we use to count cores) undercounts past 64 on Windows for the same reason. The correct fix must count cores across all processor groups **and** ensure the miner threads actually run across them — however that is best achieved.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] On a Windows machine with **more than 64 logical cores**, CPU mining uses **more than 64 threads** — up to the count the user selects, bounded by the machine's real logical core count
- [ ] Core count is determined accurately across all processor groups (not capped at 64 the way `available_parallelism()` is)
- [ ] No regression on machines with ≤64 cores, and no regression on macOS or Linux
- [ ] **The PR includes proof of a working result on real hardware:**
  - [ ] A screenshot proving the test machine's spec (Task Manager → Performance, or CPU-Z) showing **more than 64 logical cores**
  - [ ] Screenshots and/or xmrig log excerpts showing **more than 64 threads in active use** after the fix, on that machine

### Development Requirements

This bounty **cannot be developed or verified blind.** You must have access to a Windows machine with more than 64 logical cores to work on it. A fix that "looks correct" but is not demonstrated to work on qualifying hardware will **not** be accepted — the hardware proof above is mandatory, not optional. A VM/emulated core count that does not reproduce real processor-group behavior does not qualify. If you do not have such a machine, this is not the right bounty for you.

### Context

- Relevant code:
  - `src-tauri/src/mining/cpu/manager.rs` — `determine_number_of_cores_to_use()` uses `thread::available_parallelism()`, which undercounts past 64 on Windows
  - `src-tauri/src/mining/cpu/miners/xmrig.rs` — passes the count through as `--threads={cpu_threads}`
  - xmrig is pinned to `6.25.0` in `src-tauri/binaries-versions/binaries_versions_*.json`
- **Open question (see the analysis in the comment below):** it is not yet confirmed whether xmrig 6.25.0 spreads threads across processor groups on its own. The comment below is a *lead/hypothesis*, not a confirmed ceiling — do not treat it as ruling out an app-side fix. The bounty is open to any approach that demonstrably works: an accurate all-groups core count, adjusting how xmrig is launched (e.g. affinity handling on Win11/Server 2022), or a launcher strategy. What matters is the proven result on real hardware, not the mechanism.
- Reference on the 64-core threshold and Windows processor groups: https://bitsum.com/general/the-64-core-threshold-processor-groups-and-windows/

title: Create wallet benchmarks
author: SWvheerden
body:
# Bounty: Reproducible Wallet Performance Test Harness

**Tier:** L — 150,000 XTM

## Description

Build a reproducible test harness that measures `minotari-cli` wallet performance across three modes: old wallet (`minotari_console_wallet` via gRPC), new wallet (`minotari-cli` library with offline signing), and payment processor (batch 1-to-many transactions via `minotari-cli`).

Implementation approach is up to you — Rust, Python, shell scripts, or any combination — as long as the results are reproducible and verifiable by a third party running the same harness against the same network.

## Deliverables

1. **Harness source code** in a new repo, buildable and runnable by anyone with access to a funded wallet on Esmeralda testnet.
2. **Run instructions** — complete, step-by-step, no implicit knowledge.
3. **Baseline result profile** — a structured report generated by running the harness, committed alongside the code, serving as proof the harness works and as a reference point for future comparisons.

## Wallet Modes

1. **Old Wallet (`minotari_console_wallet`)** — harness manages the wallet process lifecycle (spawn, wait for ready, run tests, tear down) and interacts via gRPC.
2. **New Wallet (`minotari-cli` library)** — uses the `minotari` crate directly: local UTXO selection, `sign_locked_transaction`, broadcast via HTTP RPC to a base node. No external wallet process.
3. **Payment Processor** — uses the new wallet's batch transaction capability to send 1-to-many transactions.

## Configuration Parameters

The harness MUST expose (and the result profile MUST record) the following parameters. Values below are the reference defaults for the baseline result profile.

| Parameter | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `A_fund` | 10,000 tXTM | Single funding UTXO per mode. ~71% of one Esmeralda block reward. |
| `C_min` | 3 | Confirmation depth before a UTXO is treated as spendable. |
| `volume_target` | 512 UTXOs | Target UTXO count after S1. |
| `doubling_rounds` | 6 | Take 1 → 64 UTXOs. |
| `fanout_outputs_per_tx` | 8 | Take 64 → 512 UTXOs in one round of 64 txs. |
| `concurrent_batches` | 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 | Ramp for S4. |
| `S4_T_budget` | 15 min | Stop condition per batch in S4. |
| `S5_M` | 100 | Total recipients paid in S5. |
| `S5_K` | 10 | Outputs per batch tx in S5 (→ 10 batch txs vs. 100 individual txs). |
| `fee_rate` | pinned | Explicit fee rate passed to all modes. Record the value used. |
| Wallet binary versions | pinned | Exact commit/tag of `minotari_console_wallet`, `minotari-cli`, base node. |

**Seed strategy:** fresh seed per wallet mode. Funding the next mode's seed can come from anywhere (faucet, prior mode sweep-back, miner wallet) — the funding step is not part of the measurement.

## Test Protocol

Nine scenarios run per wallet mode, in the order below. Every scan scenario starts with a wiped wallet data dir. Every scenario records: wall-clock duration, fees paid, success/failure counts with reasons, and final balance delta vs. expected.
When you need to rescan from genesis, use the api to change the seed words so that the encoded birthday reflects 0.

### B0 — Baseline Scan (empty wallet)

Floor cost of block-walk + view-key check with nothing to store.

- **Preconditions:** fresh seed, never funded. Base node synced to tip. Birthday = 0.
- **Steps:** launch scan from genesis → wait for wallet height == tip.
- **Verification:** 0 UTXOs, 0 balance, 0 outputs found.
- **Metrics:** `T_scan`, `blocks_per_sec`, `H_tip_start`, `H_tip_end`, peak RSS, peak CPU%.

### S0 — Funding Baseline

Identical starting state for all downstream scenarios.

- **Preconditions:** fresh seed, fresh wallet data dir. Base node synced.
- **Steps:** init wallet → record birthday `H_birth` → receive 1 UTXO of `A_fund` → wait for confirmation at depth ≥ `C_min`.
- **Verification:** exactly 1 spendable UTXO; balance == `A_fund`.
- **Metrics:** broadcast→mempool time; broadcast→confirmed-at-depth time; `H_birth`, tip height.

### S1 — UTXO Build-up (doubling + fan-out → 512)

Produces on-chain history for scan scenarios AND measures per-tx cost.

**Doubling phase (6 rounds):**

| Round | Txs (serial) | Inputs/tx | Outputs/tx | UTXOs after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 |
| 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | 4 |
| 3 | 4 | 1 | 2 | 8 |
| 4 | 8 | 1 | 2 | 16 |
| 5 | 16 | 1 | 2 | 32 |
| 6 | 32 | 1 | 2 | 64 |

**Fan-out phase (1 round):** 64 txs, each 1 input → 8 outputs → 512 UTXOs.

**Per-round procedure:**
1. Snapshot balance and UTXO set.
2. Construct + broadcast all round txs serially.
3. Wait until all round txs reach depth ≥ `C_min`.
4. Refresh wallet state (tip refresh, not full scan).
5. Verify UTXO count matches target; verify `balance_after == balance_before − Σ round_fees`.

**Failure halts the scenario** — doubling cannot continue if a round's txs don't all land.

**Metrics (per tx):** construction time, broadcast→mempool time, broadcast→confirmed time, fee paid, outcome. **Per round:** wall-clock, total fees, failures. **Scenario total:** cumulative fees, cumulative wall-clock, balance reconciliation delta.

### S2 — Scan from Genesis (checkpoint 1)

- **Preconditions:** S1 complete; wipe wallet data dir; birthday = 0.
- **Steps:** launch scan from genesis → wait for height == tip.
- **Verification:** 512 spendable UTXOs rediscovered; balance matches post-S1; all S1 txs in history.
- **Metrics:** same as B0, plus outputs-found count.
- **Delta:** `T_scan(S2) − T_scan(B0)` ≈ cost of discovering/storing 512 UTXOs and their spent-input matches.

### S3 — Scan from Birthday (checkpoint 1)

Identical to S2 except **birthday = `H_birth`**. `blocks_scanned = H_tip_end − H_birth`.

### S4 — Concurrent Construction

Measures what each wallet mode does under concurrent load. Locking, serialization, selection contention, and stalls are the signal — NOT failures to engineer around.

- **Preconditions:** S1 complete.
- **Steps:** for each `N_concurrent` ∈ {8, 16, 32, 64, 128}:
  1. Pick `N_concurrent` distinct recipient addresses (self-sends OK).
  2. Fire all construction+broadcast calls in parallel (harness-level threads/async).
  3. Record per-tx: submit time, construction-complete time, broadcast outcome, confirmation time, error string.
  4. Wait for all terminal states OR `T_budget` elapsed (then record partial results and continue).
- **No retry. No backoff. No UTXO pre-partitioning.**
- **Metrics:** per-tx durations; batch wall-clock; success rate; max observed serialization gap between consecutive construction-complete events (exposes internal serialization); any double-selection rejections.

### S5 — Payment Processor Throughput

Headline comparison: batch 1-to-N vs. individual 1-to-1 sends paying the **same `M` recipients**.

- **Preconditions:** S4 complete. Record and disclose current UTXO count / balance (post-S4 state; do not normalize).
- **Recipient set:** fixed list of `M = 100` addresses, used by both arms.

**Arm A — Batch:**
- Submit `M/K = 10` batch txs (1 input → `K = 10` outputs), back-to-back.
- Wait for all confirmed at depth ≥ `C_min`.
- Record `T_batch`.

**Arm B — Individual:**
- Submit `M = 100` single-output txs, back-to-back.
- Wait for all confirmed at depth ≥ `C_min`.
- Record `T_individual`.

**Metrics:**
- `T_batch`, `T_individual`
- **Throughput multiplier = `T_individual / T_batch`** (headline)
- Total fees per arm; fee-per-recipient per arm
- Blocks consumed per arm
- Per-tx success/failure counts

**Runs per mode:** batch arm for payment processor; individual arm for new wallet and old wallet (for context).

### S6 — Scan from Genesis (checkpoint 2)

Same shape as S2 but after S5. Expected history ≈ 127 txs (S1) + S4 txs + 110 txs (S5) ≈ 250+ txs, several hundred UTXOs to rediscover.

**Delta signals:** `T_scan(S6) − T_scan(S2)` = cost of scanning S4+S5 history. `T_scan(S6) / T_scan(B0)` = scan slowdown factor vs. empty baseline.

### S7 — Scan from Birthday (checkpoint 2)

Same shape as S3 but after S5.

## Cross-cutting Metrics

Captured in every scenario:
- **Fees paid** — per tx, per round, per scenario total.
- **Error rate** — success / rejection / stall / timeout, with error strings.
- **Balance reconciliation** — `expected_balance − observed_balance` after every scenario. Flag any non-zero delta.
- **Chain tip heights** — at scenario start and end (for drift disclosure across modes).

## Result Profile (output format)

Structured output (JSON preferred, CSV acceptable), committed alongside the harness code as proof-of-run and reference baseline.

**Must include:**
- Hardware / environment disclosure: CPU model, RAM, disk type, OS, network path to base node (local vs. remote).
- Pinned versions: `minotari_console_wallet`, `minotari-cli`, base node — commit hash or release tag.
- All configuration parameter values used for the run.
- Per-scenario, per-mode block of metrics as described above.
- Computed deltas (e.g., `T_scan(S2) − T_scan(B0)`, S5 throughput multiplier).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Harness runs against Esmeralda testnet with no manual intervention beyond initial wallet funding.
- All three modes implemented; all nine scenarios (B0, S0–S7) produce results per mode.
- All configuration parameters exposed and recorded in the output.
- A third party can clone the repo, build the harness, fund the wallets, and reproduce the test — instructions are clear and complete.
- A baseline result profile is committed alongside the harness code.
- Results are output in a structured format suitable for automated comparison.
- **Harness does not hide wallet pain** (see principle below).

## Principle — Harness Measures, Does Not Engineer Around Wallet Pain

UTXO locking, selection contention, stalls, and failed tx construction under concurrency are **part of what the harness measures**. Do not add harness-level retries, backoff, UTXO pre-partitioning, throttling, or serialization that hides how a wallet mode actually behaves under load.

If a wallet stalls for 10 minutes on a locked store, that stall is the result. If a wallet mode cannot complete a scenario, that is a reportable result — not a reason to tune the harness until it does. Timeouts should be generous (so stalled-but-progressing wallets get credit for completing), but the observed behavior must show up in the metrics.

title: Write up the Exchange update process in the Tari Wiki
author: metalaureate
body:
When a release needs exchanges to act, we contact them. That process works, but it only exists in the heads of the people who do it. The community has asked us to write it down.

The deliverable is an article on wiki.tari.com covering how we run an exchange update:

- Who we contact at each exchange, and through which channel.
- What triggers an outreach, meaning which kinds of release we tell exchanges about and which we do not.
- How much notice we give.
- What the message says: version, what they need to do, and by when.
- Who at Tari Labs sends it and tracks who has responded.

title: online multiplayer lobby [bounty: 6666 XTR]
author: DreadKnight
body:
In order to have online multiplayer feature back up, we need to remove [Nakama](https://heroiclabs.com/nakama), as it was problematic and we only used it in order to match players together via its lobby feature, the rest of gameplay is actually p2p (we'll secure it via #1791).

We should even remove it as project dependency and have lobby feature implemented via Google's [Open Match](https://open-match.dev) -> [repo](https://github.com/googleforgames/open-match).
Or we could have our own implementation, not replying on something generic that's "one size fits all", there are upsides.

Could have this without a user system for the players, having auto-generated unique id's for now, later we'll go for #2032.

Open Match is serverless, so we should be able to host it via our sponsored servers provided by [Qoddi](https://qoddi.com), though Open Match uses Kubernets and [KinD](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io) is needed in order to host those on Docker -> https://github.com/googleforgames/open-match/blob/main/docs/development.md

Note that the current implementation of online multiplayer (using Nakama) hasn't been maintained and is probably broken; it was tested for a while until we bumped into a show-stopping bug that wasn't fixed #2044 since the coder couldn't figure it out and neither did others - so ideally that issue will be fixed or avoided in the process.

This is issue is the first vital step towards having online multiplayer -> https://github.com/orgs/FreezingMoon/projects/11

title: modular abilities [bounty: 70 XTR]
author: DreadKnight
body:
Unit abilities should be refactored by having a proper API, with a set of actions that can be combined.
They should have a common class that gets instantiated, standard object oriented programming style.

It should roughly contain stuff like:
- type (first ability is passive, second is a basic attack, third is a special move and forth is an ultimate)
- usability (certain conditions must be met in order to be able to use the ability, provided cost is fulfilled; an ability could be disable by a debuff; active abilities are usually only usable once per turn)
- cost (usable abilities have a usage cost, usually being a certain amount of energy points, but not exclusive or limited to that)
- upgrade (passive abilities tend to auto upgrade before a set amount of rounds, while the other require a certain number of uses before upgrading; when an ability is upgraded, certain parameters are improved)
- effect (this can be certain amounts of damage, healing, movement, buffs/debuffs)
- target (can be self, enemy units, allied units, area, hexagon, etc.)
- range (some abilities have patterns, basic attacks can usually hit in front and sideways of the first/last unit hexagon; )
- hits (some abilities can hit multiple times or even be used multiple times in the same round)
- modifiers (stats and masteries can influence the output of specific abilities)

Files to be refactored: `src/ability.js` and the stuff in `src/abilities`.
This is one of the biggest things holding back the project, as it makes it hard to code abilities for new awesome playable units.
